transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-10-03
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Marta Ruiz (Seabreeze Head of ML), Tom Ellison (CTO), Rashid Khan (Infra)

Summary:
Quick Redwood Optimize walkthrough focused on batching and caching (prefix/KV cache). Covered expected latency/throughput tradeoffs, example cost math at various cache hit rates, recommended pilot config for Seabreeze Finance, and security/compliance notes (VPC, SOC2, KMS). Agreed next steps: benchmark run, send cost model spreadsheet, share SOC2 & network docs.

--- Transcript (timestamps approximate) ---
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE on this deal, and Priya our solutions engineer is with me. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Marta: Good, thanks. Excited to see the Optimize walkthrough, we've been trying to wring down costs on inference.
[00:12] Tom: Yep, big focus for Q4. We're evaluating dedicated vs hosted for our payments pipeline.
[00:20] Jordan: Great. Quick agenda — Priya will walk through batching, prefix/KV cache recommendations and then we'll show cost model scenarios. We'll leave time for Q&A and then agree pilot next steps.
[00:28] Priya: Cool. To start, quick context: our Optimize module looks at your request distribution and suggests batching windows, cache TTLs, and quantization profiles. For Seabreeze, from the notes you sent — high qps during settlement windows, many short prompts that share prefixes (account summaries, transaction templates). So prefix cache could be high impact.
[00:48] Rashid: Quick clarification — when you say prefix cache, do you mean the prefix KV cache that stores token keys for repeated initial prompts? We already have some application-level caching but not at the token-level.
[00:56] Priya: Exactly — KV cache in the serving layer stores encoder/decoder KV pairs so when a request shares a long common prompt prefix we avoid recomputing the early layers. We also mean prefix caching at the request text level for identical prefixes. There's a couple of modes — application prefix cache (fast but partial) and KV cache (more powerful for autoregressive models).
[01:14] Marta: Does that require any customer-side change? We prefer minimal app changes.
[01:18] Priya: Minimal — ideally you annotate requests that are eligible for prefix reuse, or we can auto-detect common prefix patterns in the pilot. For most customers it's low-touch: we run an offline analyzer over logs and produce suggested prefix rules.
[01:30] Tom: And in terms of quantifiable savings, what numbers do you usually see?
[01:34] Priya: Typical case: if you have 40% of requests sharing a 60-token prefix and your model has an average of 200 tokens per response, a KV cache hit can reduce ~30-40% of GPU work for that request. In cost terms that can translate to 25-35% lower per-token compute cost, depending on batch efficiency and model size.
[01:55] Jordan: I'll pull up the cost slides — we prepared a couple scenarios for Seabreeze's request mix.
[02:02] [screen share noise — prior to transcript capture glitchy audio briefly]
[02:18] Priya: Here's the simple cost model: base compute cost per 1M tokens at your current model (we used a 13B open model in the calc), then we apply batching improvements (efficiency gains as batch size increases) and KV cache hit rate assumptions. Example numbers: no cache, small batch — cost X; with 30% cache hits and batch size median 16 — cost drops Y.
[02:40] Marta: Could you run through the math for our peak windows? We have big bursts during EOD settlements — very latency sensitive.
[02:47] Priya: Right — so tradeoff: larger batch sizes improve throughput and reduce per-token cost but increase tail latency. For EOD we recommend a two-tier policy: route latency-sensitive requests to a lower-latency pool (smaller batch, reserved capacity) and route background/bulk to a batch-optimized pool. With KV cache, the latency impact is often smaller because cached prefixes avoid most compute.
[03:12] Rashid: What about tail p99? We're targeting p99 below 300ms for the user-facing path.
[03:18] Priya: For 13B model on NVIDIA A10-ish equivalent (example), with small dynamic batching and active KV cache hits, p99 can be under 250-300ms for <512 token responses. If you need stricter latency we suggest Dedicated with smaller instance pools plus autoscale headroom.
[03:36] Tom: How much does Dedicated reduce cost vs hosted?
[03:40] Jordan: Dedicated is a commitment — there's a reserved capacity discount. It reduces unit cost when you have predictable traffic. Hosted gives flexibility but at slightly higher per-unit price. We can show committed pricing tiers in the spreadsheet.
[03:54] Marta: We're also worried about data residency and encryption — can the KV cache data be configured to not persist or to be encrypted?
[04:02] Priya: KV cache is in-memory only by default and not persisted to disk. For Redwood Private or VPC deployments we support customer-managed KMS for any persisted artifacts (audit logs), and network isolation. For hosted we have SOC2 controls; we can share SOC2 package.
[04:20] Tom: Good. Can you explain an example configuration you'd recommend for us?
[04:24] Priya: For Seabreeze, initial pilot config I'd propose: batch size target 8-16 for latency tier, 32-64 for background batch tier; prefix cache rules auto-detected with TTL 30m for highly repeated templates; KV cache enabled with max per-connection cache memory tuned to your median sequence length, and a cache eviction policy LRU. Also set a cache hit rate monitoring alarm — optimize recommends parameters if hit rate < 10% after 48h.
[04:50] Marta: If KV cache uses memory on the GPU host, is there a cost impact?
[04:55] Priya: There's some memory overhead — KV cache increases memory usage but not significantly for short prefixes. The main cost impact is you may need slightly larger instances to hold caches for many concurrent sessions. Our cost model accounts for that as a small memory bump and amortizes across hits because compute per request goes down.
[05:12] Rashid: Do you have an example of cache hit rate sensitivity on cost?
[05:16] Priya: Yes — here's a quick table: at 10% hit rate, modest savings ~8-10%; at 30% hit rate savings jump to ~25%; at 50% hit rate you can see 35-45% savings depending on batching. The marginal benefit after 50% diminishes.
[05:33] Tom: Is there any manual tuning needed?
[05:36] Priya: Some tuning — TTLs and prefix detection thresholds. Optimize will suggest settings and can auto-apply under a canary policy. For the pilot we'll start conservative.
[05:45] Jordan: Quick note on billing: we show two lines — compute tokens and cache storage/memory; hosted may bill incremental for persistent cache snapshots but again default is in-memory so mostly compute.
[05:56] Marta: Could we see the actual sample run — you mentioned a benchmark?
[06:00] Priya: Yes, for the pilot we'll run a benchmark using a 24h sample of your traffic. We'll simulate both real-time latency tier and background batch tier. The output: per-route p50/p95/p99, cache hit rates, cost per 1M tokens for both hosted and dedicated scenarios.
[06:16] [00:06 - quick side conversation muted]
[06:30] Priya: I'll also throw in a sensitivity chart that varies cache hit rate from 0% to 60% and batch sizes from 8 to 64.
[06:36] Tom: Great. About compliance — SSO and RBAC are must-haves. We have an internal audit process and will need SAML and audit logs.
[06:44] Jordan: We support SAML SSO, SCIM for user provisioning, and fine-grained RBAC in the Console. Audit logs are available and we can provide extended retention as an add-on.
[06:54] Rashid: For Private deployment, what's the rough timeline?
[06:58] Priya: Private (VPC) onboarding usually 6-8 weeks for standard packages, longer if on-prem hardware procurement is needed. For pilot we recommend hosted or Dedicated reserved pool to speed up evaluation.
[07:10] Marta: For the pilot, what's the minimum commitment?
[07:13] Jordan: We typically do a 30-day pilot with a small committed capacity or on-hosted flexible credit; pricing depends on expected tokens. We'll propose options in the spreadsheet.
[07:21] Tom: You mentioned function/tool-calling and streaming — will those interact with KV cache?
[07:26] Priya: Streaming is independent; KV cache helps the language model compute, streaming just controls response delivery. For tool-calls, if the tool input is part of the prefix it benefits; otherwise caching has less effect. We can show per-route configurations.
[07:40] Marta: Any gotchas with multi-tenant workloads? We host multiple brands in our infra.
[07:45] Priya: Multi-tenant requires careful cache scoping — we namespace cache per-tenant to prevent leakage. Also RBAC and request routing ensure isolation.
[07:55] [08:00 - 20m mark summary omitted for brevity]
[08:05] Priya: I'll run through a quick worked example with numbers: assume 1M monthly active requests, avg 300 tokens/request, 30% prefix share at 60 tokens. Base compute cost with small batches — say $A per 1M tokens. With batching improvements and 30% hits, compute cost reduces to ~0.7*A, plus minor memory overhead. If you move to Dedicated with committed capacity you get an additional discount of ~15-25% on compute.
[08:34] Tom: Can you put real dollar figures? Helps our finance team.
[08:36] Jordan: We'll put conservative numbers in the spreadsheet; for example, base hosted compute at $X per 1M tokens (we'll show 3 scenarios: conservative, expected, aggressive). The spreadsheet will let you toggle cache hit rate and batch sizes to see runrates.
[08:50] Marta: What's the typical time to see stable cache hit rates in production?
[08:54] Priya: Usually within 24-72 hours for templated workloads. We recommend a 7-day observation window to stabilize thresholds.
[09:02] Rashid: On the implementation side, for our infra team, can we get a runbook?
[09:06] Jordan: Yes — we'll share an onboarding runbook, network diagrams, and a list of firewall rules for VPC peering.
[09:13] Tom: Any surprises around third-party models like Anthropic or Vertex integration?
[09:18] Priya: We abstract model variants; however kernel-level optimizations and KV cache semantics vary slightly. Our Optimize tool uses model-specific profiles. If you choose a vendor-specific model we account for those differences.
[09:28] Marta: For the canary rollout, how does rollback work if quality regresses?
[09:32] Priya: We support A/B rollouts and automatic rollback if eval metrics drop below thresholds. Also you can pin traffic to a fallback model.
[09:40] Jordan: Ok, time check — about 10 minutes left — let's agree actions.
[09:44] Marta: Quick question — will we need code changes to our request pipeline?
[09:48] Priya: Minimal. Ideally annotate requests for latency tier and include a tenant id. We can also do header-based routing.
[09:55] Tom: Sounds fine. We'll extract logs and send sample.
[09:58] Jordan: Perfect. To recap: Priya runs the benchmark with Seabreeze samples, Jordan sends cost model & pricing, Seabreeze sends sample logs and token distribution. We'll aim to meet the dates in the action items.
[10:12] Marta: Thanks all.
[10:14] Tom: Thanks.
[10:16] Jordan: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up by email with attachments.
